name: U.S. Factor's House

documented_range.note:
THREE WITNESSES ACROSS EIGHTEEN YEARS, AND NOT ONE OF THEM DATES THE BUILDING. The range opens 1 January 1818 because that is the year Gurdon Hubbard reached Chicago and the year his inventory of the place describes (`bk_hub_063`, leaf 76, printed p. 38); the house he found was older — he has Jouett in it as United States factor 'from 1804 to about the year 1810' and John Dean succeeding him 'at the second construction of the fort' — so 1818 IS A FLOOR ON THE RECORD AND NOT A CONSTRUCTION DATE, and no source this project holds gives one. What stands between that floor and the scene is two further sightings: Hurlbut has the American Fur Company buy 'the Factory House, located just south of Fort Dearborn' from the United States in 1822 and Jean Baptiste Beaubien move his family into it (`bk_afc_009`), and the Harrison plan of 24 February 1830 letters `U.S. Factor's House` against the three blocks this record's position is read from.

IT CLOSES 29 DECEMBER 1836, the evacuation, and that is the same floor every Fort Dearborn record here carries rather than a demolition: nothing attests when the reservation's buildings came down.

WHAT CARRIES THE SCENE DATE OF 1 JULY 1835 is the middle of that range and not either end. A building three independent texts have standing in 1818, 1822 and 1830 is standing five years after the last of them unless something says it stopped, and nothing does. THAT ARGUMENT IS STRONGER HERE THAN AT THE OUT BUILDINGS NEXT DOOR, which rest on the plate alone; it is still an argument from silence about the last five years, and the grade says so. A fourth fact bears on the same five years without being read as occupancy: the Illinois land-sale register has John Baptist Baubian entering this ground on 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene — a pre-emption entry over the reservation, which is a transaction and not a sighting of a house.

position.symbolic_location: On the Fort Dearborn reservation 152 m south of the palisade's nearest corner, east of the only road out of the fort and off the garrison garden's southern corner.
position.note:
THE PLATE GIVES THE COORDINATE AND HUBBARD CORROBORATES THE GROUND. Read off the 1830 Harrison plan by the transform T-0883 stated and T-0882 reused, unchanged and not re-derived here: Internet Archive leaf n242 of historyofchicago01andr (Andreas, History of Chicago, vol. 1, p. 113), rotated 90 degrees anticlockwise so the sheet's own true-north arrow stands vertical, 2715 x 2003 px, anchor pixel (1445, 644) on the committed palisade centre at local E +1152.0, N +221.0, at 0.33528 m/px. The full reading, its per-block pixels and its four checks are `data/traces/harrison_1830_us_factors_house.json`; this note does not repeat them.

THE PIXEL. The plate letters `U.S. Factor's House` in three lines against THREE solid blocks, and this record is block A — the one the label touches, and the largest. Its ink centres at pixel (1445.6, 1194.5), which is 0.2 m east and 184.6 m south of the enclosure centre: local ENU (1152.2, 36.4), UTM 448224.90 E, 4637432.20 N. CARRY +/-20 % on size and +/-25 m on position, exactly as every plate-derived record here does — the sheet has no scale bar and its own source record says it is used for arrangement and proportion rather than absolute size.

WHY BLOCK A AND NOT THE GROUP CENTRE. The label stands beside A and could as easily name all three (the trace says so and does not pretend otherwise), but A is what this record builds, so A's own ink is what it stands on. The group centre is 6.7 m away — well inside the +/-25 m this plate carries — so nothing turns on the choice except honesty about which pixels were measured.

WHERE IT STANDS RELATIVE TO THE FORT AND THE ROAD. 152 m south of the palisade's southernmost corner and 182 m south of its centre: outside the pickets, inside the fence line `bk_hub_060` runs from river to river, about 48 m south of the Gate the same plate letters in that fence, and east of the road band whose north-west edge is the committed garrison garden's south-east face. That is where Hubbard independently puts it — 'Just east of the road, and adjoining the fence running east to the river' — and Hubbard never saw this plate.

THE BEARING IS THE DRAWN ONE; WHICH LONG WALL IS THE FRONT IS NOT. The block's long axis runs at 40 degrees anticlockwise from east, which is a bearing of 50 degrees, and that is measured. `rotation_deg` 320 faces the facade north-west, onto the road the house stood 'just east of'; the opposite choice, 140, gives the identical footprint and moves only the openings. It is INVENTED and it is covered at L231.

IT IS NOT `jb_beaubien_homestead`. That record stands at local (1133.2, 177.8), 139.7 m north of this one, and carried this building's identity as an alias until T-0894 measured the separation. The alias came off there; this is the ground the plate actually letters.

derivation.reason: The two machine-checkable methods this project holds are a platted corner and a traced waterline, and this is neither: it is a pixel offset on a re-engraved plate, hung on a fort centre that is itself an inference, on ground the 1834 plat does not subdivide. The whole rule is written out above and in the trace — the leaf, the orientation, the anchor, the scale and the pixel — so it is reproducible by hand; declaring a derivation method that could not recompute it would be worse than declaring none.

footprint.note: NO SOURCE GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION. 20.4 x 7.9 m is block A's own principal extents on the plate — about 67 x 26 ft at the derived 1.10 ft/px — and it wants the same +/-20 % as everything else off this sheet. THE BLOCK IS DRAWN AS A HEAVY OUTLINED BAR whose engraved fill has broken up on this impression, so the second moments were taken over the outline and the surviving fill together and the figure is the BAR, not a wall thickness; it is a ceiling on the building rather than an estimate of it. The long side runs at bearing 50 degrees as drawn. THE SIZE IS THE ONE MEASURED THING THAT ARGUES FOR THE IDENTIFICATION rather than merely surviving it: 67 x 26 ft is a government trading house with a store and a dwelling in it, and it is the only one of the plate's three blocks that Hubbard's two storeys will fit.

construction.note: ATTESTED IN THE WORD, and it is the rarest thing on this record. `bk_hub_063`: 'a two-story, SQUARED-LOG structure'. Squared — hewn, not round — is what this archetype builds, so the fabric here is read and not invented, which is the difference between this building and the two out buildings 130 m north of it whose `log` is recorded at L228 as pure default.

stories.note: HUBBARD SAYS TWO STOREYS OF THE FACTOR HOUSE; THIS RECORD SAYS THEY ARE BLOCK A'S, AND THAT SECOND STEP IS THE INFERENCE. The prose names one building — 'the "Factor House", a two-story, squared-log structure' — and the plate letters that name against three blocks, so which of the three carries the storeys is not on the sheet. A is taken to be it on two grounds stated rather than assumed: the label's first letter stands about 2 m clear of A's north-east end and touches no other block, and A at 20.4 x 7.9 m is the only one of the three a two-storey dwelling-and-store will fit (B is a 16.6 x 5.1 m bar set across it, C is 6.7 x 5.0 m). Neither ground is proof and the grade is `inferred` because of it. THE ALTERNATIVE THE TICKET ALLOWED — 'not determinable, so the storey count is inferred from the type' — would have put ONE storey here on no evidence at all while a witness was sitting on the shelf saying two; taking the witness and writing down exactly how far it had to be carried is the better of the two answers, and this note is that distance.

wall_height_m.note: NO HEIGHT IS ATTESTED for this building or for any building at this post. 5.2 m is two storeys of about 8 ft 6 in in the clear, the archetype's own band for a two-storey log core. Invented.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the archetype's default and the only alternative it builds is a shed, which is not a form a two-storey dwelling takes. Invented.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building at this fort. Invented, at the archetype's default.

chimneys.note: No stack is attested. One is the archetype's default and the smallest claim available for a heated two-storey dwelling; a 20 m building could as easily have carried two, and the record does not guess upward. Invented.

phases.change_note: ONE PHASE, AND THE BUILDING CHANGED HANDS TWICE INSIDE IT. Jouett to Dean at the second construction of the fort, then the United States to the American Fur Company in 1822 with Beaubien moving in; not one of the three witnesses describes any change to the fabric, so nothing here is dated to those transfers. The name on the record is the plate's, which is the name the sheet letters.

function.note: THE FUNCTION IS THE NAME AND EVERY WITNESS USES IT. A United States factory was the government's own trading house — the post at which the Indian trade was carried on the government's account — and all three sources name it as such: the plate letters `U.S. Factor's House`, Hubbard has it occupied 'by a Mr. Jouett, United States factor', and Hurlbut has the American Fur Company buying 'the Factory House' from the United States. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED IS WHAT WENT ON INSIDE IT IN 1835. The factory system was abolished in 1822, which is the same year Hurlbut has the building sold out of government hands; by the scene date this is a private house that used to be a trading house, and nothing this project holds says whether any trade was still carried on in it.

research_note:
PLACED UNDER T-1036, OUT OF A READING THAT REFUSED TO PLACE IT. T-0894 measured the three blocks the 1830 Harrison plan letters `U.S. Factor's House` and deliberately built nothing, because the plate gives arrangement and a +/-20 % size and no material, no roof, no opening and no way to say which block carries Hubbard's two storeys. This ticket is that refusal re-examined with the prose read alongside the plate instead of after it, and two of the four gaps close: `bk_hub_063` gives the fabric in a word — SQUARED-LOG — and gives the storeys, and the size of block A is what lets the storeys be attached to a particular block rather than to a group. The roof and the openings do not close and are invented at L231.

WHY ONE BLOCK AND NOT THREE. The label touches A; both prose witnesses describe ONE building and neither mentions a group; A is the only one of the three that a two-storey squared-log dwelling-and-store fits. B (16.6 x 5.1 m, set across A 12 m to the north-west) and C (6.7 x 5.0 m, 15 m to the south-west) are DRAWN AND UNLETTERED, and they are refused as fabric rather than omitted: a government factory had a store, a warehouse, a stable and a smith about it, the sheet says something stood on those two footprints, and it cannot say which of those things either was. Building them would be two invented buildings hung on one label — the shape `docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md` refuses for the Well and the Cultivated Field, and the shape this ticket exists to avoid. Their measurements are banked in the trace so a source that names them turns a footprint into a building without re-reading the plate.

AND THE SPLIT-PICKET FENCE IS NOT BUILT. `bk_hub_063` gives the Factor House 'a neat split-picket fence' and the Jouett grave 50 m away got its fence built off the same clause at L229, so the refusal needs its reason on the record. Three things separate the two cases. FIRST, THE PLATE'S SILENCE MEANS SOMETHING HERE AND MEANS NOTHING THERE: this sheet draws the three blocks and draws no enclosure round any of them, while it DOES draw the garrison garden's zigzag fence and John Crafts's Lot's property lines — at the grave it drew a name and nothing else, so its silence about a fence carried no weight. SECOND, A GRAVE PLOT HAS A SIZE AND A HOUSE YARD DOES NOT: L229 invented 10 x 8 ft around a burial, which is the size a burial is; the extent of a yard round a 20 m building is unbounded by anything, so the invention would be the largest single dimension on this ticket rather than its smallest. THIRD, HUBBARD IS DESCRIBING 1818 — the fence is a government establishment's, and the house had been thirteen years in private hands by the scene date. THIS IS NOT A JUDGEMENT THAT THERE WAS NO FENCE. It is a statement that this project cannot say where it ran; `docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md` § 7 carries it as attested-and-not-built, and a plat or a survey that draws the yard turns it into an enclosure record beside the grave's.

WHAT IS WEAK, STATED PLAINLY. The position is one plate, five years before the scene, with no scale bar, admitting on its own face to 'additions and changes suggested by the Memory of Early Settlers'. The size is a ceiling read off broken ink. The storeys are a witness carried one step across a label. Everything above the eave is invented. WHAT IS STRONG is that three independent texts put a building of this kind on this ground, that the transform lands the garrison garden within 2.3 m of where it is already committed, and that the prose and the plate agree about the road without either having seen the other. WHAT WOULD IMPROVE IT: a factory return or an Office of Indian Trade inventory for Chicago 1805-1822, a post return naming the building, the 1835 pre-emption case papers over the reservation, or any second plan of this ground.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS 102 m: this footprint stands that far inside the tract's nearest boundary, which is more than twice the working horizontal uncertainty of anything traced off the 1834 sheets (about 20 m), so the assignment survives the error the construction carries. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.
land_owner.tract: the south-west fractional quarter of section 10
